neighbours.label: Concessive ', while' or ', though' right after a claim noun in scholarly debate ('that conclusion, while ...'); the same structure about ordinary things stays quiet.
fire: Hale and his team argued the pottery was traded. But that interpretation, while intriguing, has been questioned by others.
Several authors favour a late date. Yet that reading, while attractive, relies on one damaged tablet.
Reed proposed that the migration was seasonal. That suggestion, while appealing, has little support in the data.
The model predicts a sharp fall. This prediction, while striking, depends on a single estimate.
Critics call the treaty a turning point. That judgment, while popular, overlooks the earlier talks.
Kim and colleagues inferred an early origin. But this inference, while tempting, has been disputed by geneticists.
Some scholars see a direct influence. That view, though widely held, cannot be proved from the letters.
The authors conclude that diet explains it. That explanation, while neat, ignores the role of exercise.
quiet: Hale and his team bought the pottery at auction. But that cottage, while charming, has been empty for years.
Several guests favour a late dinner. Yet that kitchen, while attractive, relies on one small oven.
Reed noticed that the bus was late. That driver, while friendly, has little patience with tourists.
The shop sells a cheap bike. This bike, while sturdy, weighs a lot on hills.
Tourists call the square a delight. That fountain, while popular, closes in the winter months.
Kim and colleagues rented an old van. But this van, while roomy, has been parked outside for weeks.
Some children see a big dog. That dog, though very large, cannot jump over the fence.
The owners say that rent is high. That apartment, while neat, lacks a view of the sea.
